Existence of Traveling wave solutions of parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis systems

Rachidi B. Salako Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Statistics Affiliation: Auburn University    Wenxian Shen Affiliation: Auburn University, AL 36849 Affiliation: U.S.A.
Abstract

The current paper is devoted to the study of traveling wave solutions of the following parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system,

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+u(a−bu),x∈ℝNτvt=Δv−v+u,x∈ℝN,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+u(a-bu),\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{N},\end{cases}

where u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) represents the population density of a mobile species and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) represents the population density of a chemoattractant, and χ\chi represents the chemotaxis sensitivity.

In an earlier work ([32]) by the authors of the current paper, traveling wave solutions of the above chemotaxis system with τ=0\tau=0 are studied. It is shown in [32] that for every 0<χ<b20<\chi<\frac{b}{2}, there is c∗​(χ)c^{*}(\chi) such that for every c>c∗​(χ)c>c^{*}(\chi) and ξ∈SN−1\xi\in S^{N-1}, the system has a traveling wave solution (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(U⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t,τ),V⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t,τ))(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(U(x\cdot\xi-ct;\tau),V(x\cdot\xi-ct;\tau)) with speed cc connecting the constant solutions (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) and (0,0)(0,0). Moreover,

limχ→0+c∗​(χ)={2​aif0<a≤11+aifa>1.\lim_{\chi\to 0+}c^{*}(\chi)=\begin{cases}2\sqrt{a}\qquad\ \text{if}\quad 0<a\leq 1\cr 1+a\qquad\text{if}\qquad a>1.\end{cases}

We prove in the current paper that for every τ>0\tau>0, there is 0<χτ∗<b20<\chi_{\tau}^{*}<\frac{b}{2} such that for every 0<χ<χτ∗0<\chi<\chi_{\tau}^{*}, there exist two positive numbers c∗⁣∗​(χ,τ)>c∗​(χ,τ)≥2​ac^{**}(\chi,\tau)>c^{*}(\chi,\tau)\geq 2\sqrt{a} satisfying that for every c∈(c∗​(χ,τ),c∗⁣∗​(χ,τ))c\in(c^{*}(\chi,\tau)\ ,\ c^{**}(\chi,\tau)) and ξ∈SN−1\xi\in S^{N-1}, the system has a traveling wave solution (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(U⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t,τ),V⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t,τ))(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(U(x\cdot\xi-ct;\tau),V(x\cdot\xi-ct;\tau)) with speed cc connecting the constant solutions (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) and (0,0)(0,0), and it does not have such traveling wave solutions of speed less than 2​a2\sqrt{a}. Moreover,

limχ→0+c∗⁣∗​(χ,τ)=∞,\lim_{\chi\to 0+}c^{**}(\chi,\tau)=\infty,
limχ→0+c∗​(χ,τ)={2​aif0<a≤1+τ​a(1−τ)+1+τ​a(1−τ)++a​(1−τ)+1+τ​aifa≥1+τ​a(1−τ)+,\lim_{\chi\to 0+}c^{*}(\chi,\tau)=\begin{cases}2\sqrt{a}\qquad\qquad\qquad\ \text{if}\quad 0<a\leq\frac{1+\tau a}{(1-\tau)_{+}}\cr\frac{1+\tau a}{(1-\tau)_{+}}+\frac{a(1-\tau)_{+}}{1+\tau a}\quad\text{if}\quad a\geq\frac{1+\tau a}{(1-\tau)_{+}},\end{cases}

and

limx→∞U⁡(x,τ)e−μ​x=1,\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{U(x;\tau)}{e^{-\mu x}}=1,

where μ\mu is the only solution of the equation μ+aμ=c\mu+\frac{a}{\mu}=c in the interval (0,min⁡{a,1+τ​a(1−τ)+})(0\ ,\ \min\{\sqrt{a},\sqrt{\frac{1+\tau a}{(1-\tau)_{+}}}\}). Furthermore,

limτ→0+χτ∗=b2,limτ→0+c∗​(χ,τ)=c∗​(χ),limτ→0+c∗⁣∗​(χ,τ)=∞.\lim_{\tau\to 0+}\chi_{\tau}^{*}=\frac{b}{2},\quad\lim_{\tau\to 0+}c^{*}(\chi;\tau)=c^{*}(\chi),\quad\lim_{\tau\to 0+}c^{**}(\chi;\tau)=\infty.

Key words. parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system, logistic source, spreading speed, traveling wave solution.

1 Introduction

At the beginning of 1970s, Keller and Segel (see [20], [21]) introduced systems of partial differential equations of the following form to model the time evolution of the density u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) of a mobile species and the density v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) of a chemoattractant,

{ut=∇⋅(m(u)∇u−χ(u,v)∇v)+f(u,v),x∈Ωτ​vt=Δ​v+g⁡(u,v),x∈Ω\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(m(u)\nabla u-\chi(u,v)\nabla v)+f(u,v),\quad x\in\Omega\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v+g(u,v),\quad x\in\Omega\end{cases} (1.1)

complemented with certain boundary condition on ∂Ω\partial\Omega if Ω\Omega is bounded, where Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{N} is an open domain; τ≥0\tau\geq 0 is a non-negative constant linked to the speed of diffusion of the chemical; the function χ⁡(u,v)\chi(u,v) represents the sensitivity with respect to chemotaxis; and the functions ff and gg model the growth of the mobile species and the chemoattractant, respectively. In literature, (1.1) is called the Keller-Segel model or a chemotaxis model.

Since the works by Keller and Segel, a rich variety of mathematical models for studying chemotaxis has appeared (see [3], [9], [10], [16], [19], [29], [37], [38], [39], [41], [45], [46], [47], [48], [49], [50], [51], and the references therein). In the current paper and the further coming papers, we will investigate various dynamical aspects of the following parabolic-parabolic Keller-Segel systems,

{ut=Δu−χ∇(u∇v)+u(a−bu),x∈ℝNτvt=Δv−v+u,x∈ℝN.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla(u\nabla v)+u(a-bu),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}.\end{cases} (1.2)

Note that, in the absence of the chemotaxis (i.e. χ=0\chi=0), the first equation of (1.2) becomes

ut=Δ​u+u⁡(a−b​u),x∈ℝN,u_{t}=\Delta u+u(a-bu),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}, (1.3)

which is referred to as Fisher or KPP equation due to the pioneering works by Fisher ([11]) and Kolmogorov, Petrowsky, Piscunov ([22]). Among important solutions of (1.3) are traveling wave solutions of (1.3) connecting the constant solutions a/ba/b and 00. It is well known that (1.3) has traveling wave solutions u⁡(t,x)=ϕ⁡(x−c​t)u(t,x)=\phi(x-ct) connecting ab\frac{a}{b} and 00 (i.e. (ϕ⁡(−∞)=a/bCLOSE(\phi(-\infty)=a/b, OPENϕ⁡(∞)=0)\phi(\infty)=0)) for all speeds c≥2​ac\geq 2\sqrt{a} and has no such traveling wave solutions of slower speed (see [11, 22, 43]). Moreover, the stability of traveling wave solutions of (1.3) connecting ab\frac{a}{b} and 00 has also been studied (see [8], [34], [40], etc.). The above mentioned results for (1.3) have also been well extended to reaction diffusion equations of the form,

ut=Δ​u+u​f​(t,x,u),x∈ℝN,u_{t}=\Delta u+uf(t,x,u),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}, (1.4)

where f⁡(t,x,u)<0f(t,x,u)<0 for u≫1u\gg 1, ∂uf⁡(t,x,u)<0\partial_{u}f(t,x,u)<0 for u≥0u\geq 0 (see [4, 5, 6, 7, 12, 13, 24, 25, 27, 30, 31, 35, 36, 43, 44, 52], etc.).

Similar to (1.3), traveling wave solutions connecting the constant solutions (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0) are among most important solutions of (1.2). However, such solutions have been hardly studied. The objective of the current paper is to study the existence of traveling wave solutions connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0). A nonnegative solution (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))(u(x,t),v(x,t)) of (1.2) is called a traveling wave solution connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0) and propagating in the direction ξ∈SN−1\xi\in S^{N-1} with speed cc if it is of the form (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(U⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t),V⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t))(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(U(x\cdot\xi-ct),V(x\cdot\xi-ct)) with limz→−∞(U⁡(z),V⁡(z))=(a/b,a/b)\lim_{z\to-\infty}(U(z),V(z))=(a/b,a/b) and limz→∞(U⁡(z),V⁡(z))=(0,0)\lim_{z\to\infty}(U(z),V(z))=(0,0).

Observe that, if (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(U⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t),V⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t))(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(U(x\cdot\xi-ct),V(x\cdot\xi-ct)) (x∈ℝN,t≥0)(x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\ t\geq 0) is a traveling wave solution of (1.2) connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0) and propagating in the direction ξ∈SN−1\xi\in S^{N-1}, then (u,v)=(U⁡(x−c​t),V⁡(x−c​t))(u,v)=(U(x-ct),V(x-ct)) (x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}}) is a traveling wave solution of

{ut=ux​x−χ​(u​vx)x+u⁡(a−b​u),x∈ℝτ​vt=vx​x−v+u,x∈ℝ\begin{cases}u_{t}=u_{xx}-\chi(uv_{x})_{x}+u(a-bu),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}\\ \tau v_{t}=v_{xx}-v+u,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}\end{cases} (1.5)

connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0). Conversely, if (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(U⁡(x−c​t),V⁡(x−c​t))(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(U(x-ct),V(x-ct)) (x∈ℝ,t≥0x\in{\mathbb{R}},\ t\geq 0) is a traveling wave solution of (1.5) connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0), then (u,v)=(U⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t),V⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t))(u,v)=(U(x\cdot\xi-ct),V(x\cdot\xi-ct)) (x∈ℝN)(x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}) is a traveling wave solution of (1.2) connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0) and propagating in the direction ξ∈SN−1\xi\in S^{N-1}. In the following, we will then study the existence of traveling wave solutions of (1.5) connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0).

Observe also that, (u,v)=(U⁡(x−c​t),V⁡(x−c​t))(u,v)=(U(x-ct),V(x-ct)) is a traveling wave solution of (1.5) connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0) if and only if (u,v)=(U⁡(x),V⁡(x))(u,v)=(U(x),V(x)) is a stationary solution of the following parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system,

{ut=ux​x+c​ux−χ​(u​vx)x+u⁡(a−b​u),x∈ℝτvt=vx​x+τcvx−v+u,x∈ℝ,\begin{cases}u_{t}=u_{xx}+cu_{x}-\chi(uv_{x})_{x}+u(a-bu),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}\\ \tau v_{t}=v_{xx}+\tau cv_{x}-v+u,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}},\end{cases} (1.6)

and (u,v)=(U⁡(x),V⁡(x))(u,v)=(U(x),V(x)) is also a stationary solution of the following parabolic-elliptic chemotaxis system,

{ut=ux​x+c​ux−χ​(u​vx)x+u⁡(a−b​u),x∈ℝ0=vx​x+τcvx−v+u,x∈ℝ.\begin{cases}u_{t}=u_{xx}+cu_{x}-\chi(uv_{x})_{x}+u(a-bu),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}\\ 0=v_{xx}+\tau cv_{x}-v+u,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}.\end{cases} (1.7)

Clearly, (1.6) and (1.7) have same stationary solutions. In this paper, to study the existence of traveling wave solutions of (1.5), we study the existence of constant cc’s so that (1.7) has a stationary solution (U⁡(x),V⁡(x))(U(x),V(x)) with (U⁡(−∞),V⁡(−∞))=(a/b,a/b)(U(-\infty),V(-\infty))=(a/b,a/b) and (U⁡(∞),V⁡(∞))=(0,0)(U(\infty),V(\infty))=(0,0).

then c∗​(χ,τ)=2​ac^{*}(\chi;\tau)=2\sqrt{a} (see Remark 4.7).

(ii)

For given τ>0\tau>0 and χ≥0\chi\geq 0, let (cmin∗​(χ,τ),cmax∗​(χ,τ))(c_{\min}^{*}(\chi,\tau),c_{\max}^{*}(\chi,\tau)) be the largest subinterval of (0,∞)(0,\infty) such that (c∗​(χ,τ),c∗⁣∗​(χ,τ))⊂(cmin∗​(χ,τ),cmax∗​(χ,τ))(c^{*}(\chi,\tau),c^{**}(\chi;\tau))\subset(c_{\min}^{*}(\chi,\tau),c_{\max}^{*}(\chi,\tau)) and for any c∈(cmin∗​(χ,τ),cmax∗​(χ,τ))c\in(c_{\min}^{*}(\chi,\tau),c_{\max}^{*}(\chi,\tau)), (1.5) has a traveling wave solution connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0) with speed cc. By Theorems C and D, for 0<χ<χτ∗0<\chi<\chi_{\tau}^{*},

2​a≤cmin∗​(χ,τ)≤c∗​(χ,τ)<c∗⁣∗​(χ,τ)≤cmax∗​(χ,τ).2\sqrt{a}\leq c_{\min}^{*}(\chi,\tau)\leq c^{*}(\chi,\tau)<c^{**}(\chi,\tau)\leq c_{\max}^{*}(\chi,\tau).

It remains also open whether cmin∗​(χ,τ)=2​ac_{\min}^{*}(\chi,\tau)=2\sqrt{a} and whether cmax∗​(χ,τ)=∞c_{\max}^{*}(\chi,\tau)=\infty. The first question is about whether the chemotaxis increases the minimal wave speed and the second question is about whether the chemotaxis prevents the existence of traveling wave solutions with large speeds. It is of great theoretical and biological interests to investigate these two questions.

Because of the lack of comparison principle, the proofs of Theorems C is highly non trivial. Note that very few results are known about the dynamics of solutions of (1.2) when a>0,b>0a>0,\ b>0 and τ>0\tau>0 for initial data which are bounded and uniformly continuous. To our best knowledge, there is no existing results on the stability of the trivial solution (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) of (1.2) when τ>0\tau>0. This makes the study of traveling wave solutions of (1.2) more complicated.

Our first key step toward the proof Theorem C is the relationship between traveling wave solutions of (1.5) and stationary solutions of (1.7). We have that (u,v)=(U⁡(x−c​t),V⁡(x−c​t))(u,v)=(U(x-ct),V(x-ct)) is traveling wave solution of (1.5) connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0) if and only if (u,v)=(U⁡(x),V⁡(x))(u,v)=(U(x),V(x)) is a stationary solution of (1.7) connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0). This observation leads to the study of the dynamics of solutions to (1.7). Concerning (1.7), we first establish Theorem A, which provides, for given cc, sufficient conditions for the existence global classical solutions. Next, we establish Theorem B, which provides, for given cc, sufficient conditions for the stability of the constant solution (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) with respect to positive perturbations for (1.7).

The proof of Theorem C involves the proof of the existence of cc such that (1.7) has stationary solutions connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0). The proof of which is based on the construction of a bounded convex non-empty subset of Cunifb​(ℝ)C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}), called ℰμ,τ​(C0)\mathcal{E}_{\mu,\tau}(C_{0}) (see (3.6)), and a continuous and compact function U:ℰμ,τ​(C0)→ℰτ,μ​(C0)U:\mathcal{E}_{\mu,\tau}(C_{0})\to\mathcal{E}_{\tau,\mu}(C_{0}). Any fixed point of this function, whose existence is guaranteed by the Schauder’s fixed theorem, becomes a stationary solution of (1.7) connecting (a/b,a/b)(a/b,a/b) and (0,0)(0,0). The construction of the set ℰτ,μ​(C0)\mathcal{E}_{\tau,\mu}(C_{0}) itself is also based on the construction of two special functions. These two special functions are sub-solution and sup-solution of a collection of parabolic equations. The proof of Theorem D utilizes some principal eigenvalue theory for elliptic equations.

In our future works, we plan to study local/global existence of classical solutions, asymptotic behaviors, and spatial spreading speeds of classical solutions of (1.2) with τ>0\tau>0 for nonnegative, bounded and uniformly continuous initial. These questions are very important in the understanding of dynamics of (1.2). When τ=0\tau=0, we refer the reader to [33] and the references therein.

It should be mentioned that there are several studies of (1.2) on bounded domains (see [48] and the references therein). When Ω\Omega is a convex bounded domain, it is known that when the logistic damping coefficient is large enough, then the constant solution (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) is stable (see [48]). It should be also pointed out that there are many studies on traveling wave solutions of several other types of chemotaxis models, see, for example, [1, 2, 15, 18, 23, 26, 28, 42], etc. In particular, the reader is referred to the review paper [42].

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 is to study the dynamics of the induced parabolic-elliptic chemotaxis system (1.7) and prove Theorems A and B. Section 3 is to establish the tools that will be needed in the proof of Theorem C. It is here that we define the two special functions, which are sub-solution and sup-solution of a collection of parabolic equations, and the non-empty bounded and convex subset ℰτ,μ​(C0)\mathcal{E}_{\tau,\mu}(C_{0}). In section 4, we study the existence and nonexistence of traveling wave solutions and prove Theorems C and D.

4 Traveling wave solutions

In this section we study the existence and nonexistence of traveling wave solutions of (1.7) connecting (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) and (0,0)(0,0), and prove Theorems C and D.

4.1 Proof of Theorem C

In this subsection, we prove Theorem C. To this end, we first prove the following important result.

Theorem 4.1.

Let a>0a>0 and b>0b>0 be given. Suppose that τ>0\tau>0, 0<χ<10<\chi<1 and 0<μ<min⁡{a,1+τ​a(1−τ)+}0<\mu<\min\{\sqrt{a},\sqrt{\frac{1+\tau a}{(1-\tau)_{+}}}\} satisfy (3.9). Then (1.5) has a traveling wave solution (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(U⁡(x−cμ​t),V⁡(x−cμ​t))(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(U(x-c_{\mu}t),V(x-c_{\mu}t)) satisfying

limx→−∞U⁡(x)=abandlimx→∞U⁡(x)e−μ​x=1\lim_{x\to-\infty}U(x)=\frac{a}{b}\quad\text{and}\quad\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{U(x)}{e^{-\mu x}}=1

where cμ=μ+aμc_{\mu}=\mu+\frac{a}{\mu}.

Our key idea to prove the above theorem is to prove that, for any τ>0\tau>0, 0<μ<min⁡{a,1+τ​a(1−τ)+}0<\mu<\min\{\sqrt{a},\sqrt{\frac{1+\tau a}{(1-\tau)_{+}}}\} and 0<χ<10<\chi<1 satisfying (3.9), there is u∗​(⋅)∈ℰτ,μ​(C~0)u^{*}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{E}_{\tau,\mu}(\tilde{C}_{0}) such that (U⁡(⋅),V⁡(⋅))=(u∗​(⋅),V⁡(⋅,u∗))(U(\cdot),V(\cdot))=(u^{*}(\cdot),V(\cdot;u^{*})) is a stationary solution of (1.7) with c=cμc=c_{\mu}, where V⁡(⋅,u∗)V(\cdot;u^{*}) is given by (3.8), and u∗​(−∞)=abu^{*}(-\infty)=\frac{a}{b} and u∗​(∞)=0u^{*}(\infty)=0, which implies that (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(u∗​(x−cμ​t),V⁡(x−cμ​t,u∗))(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(u^{*}(x-c_{\mu}t),V(x-c_{\mu}t;u^{*})) is a traveling wave solution of (1.5) connecting (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) and (0,0)(0,0) with speed c=cμc=c_{\mu}.

We now prove Theorem 4.1.

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Following the proof of Theorem 3.1 in [32], let us consider the normed linear space ℰ=Cunifb​(ℝ)\mathcal{E}=C^{b}_{\rm unif}({\mathbb{R}}) endowed with the norm

‖u‖∗=∑n=1∞12n​‖u‖L∞​([−n,n]).\|u\|_{\ast}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n}}\|u\|_{L^{\infty}([-n,\ n])}.

For every u∈ℰτ,μ​(C0)u\in\mathcal{E}_{\tau,\mu}(C_{0}) we have that

Hence ℰτ,μ​(C0)\mathcal{E}_{\tau,\mu}(C_{0}) is a bounded convex subset of ℰ\mathcal{E}. Furthermore, since the convergence in ℰ\mathcal{E} implies the pointwise convergence, then ℰτ,μ​(C0)\mathcal{E}_{\tau,\mu}(C_{0}) is a closed, bounded, and convex subset of ℰ\mathcal{E}. Furthermore, a sequence of functions in ℰτ,μ​(C0)\mathcal{E}_{\tau,\mu}(C_{0}) converges with respect to norm ∥⋅∥∗\|\cdot\|_{\ast} if and only if it converges locally uniformly convergence on ℝ{\mathbb{R}}.

for every n≥1n\geq 1. Which implies that the sequence {U⁡(⋅,un)}n≥1\{U(\cdot;u_{n})\}_{n\geq 1} is equicontinuous. The Arzela-Ascoli’s Theorem implies that there is a subsequence {U⁡(⋅,un′)}n≥1\{U(\cdot;u_{n^{\prime}})\}_{n\geq 1} of the sequence {U⁡(⋅,un)}n≥1\{U(\cdot;u_{n})\}_{n\geq 1} and a function U∈C⁡(ℝ)U\in C({\mathbb{R}}) such that {U⁡(⋅,un′)}n≥1\{U(\cdot;u_{n^{\prime}})\}_{n\geq 1} converges to UU locally uniformly on ℝ{\mathbb{R}}.
